newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Hague court hears call for leniency for Bosnia Serb.
newsitem.headline: Hague court hears call for leniency for Bosnia Serb.

text.p: A U.N. war crimes prosecutor recommended on Wednesday that a young Bosnian Croat who took part in a massacre of Moslems from Srebrenica in July 1995 should be given a jail term of no more than 10 years.

Mark Harmon of the United States urged the Hague-based U.N. war crimes tribunal to show leniency to Drazen Erdemovic on the grounds he had provided information about war crimes, had surrendered freely, had admitted his guilt and shown remorse.
"The prosecutor recommends leniency in the case of Mr Erdemovic. If it is the decision...to impose a term of imprisonment, we would respectfully recommend that it not exceed 10 years," Harmon said.
The tribunal, created by the U.N. Security Council in May 1993, may pass a maximum sentence of life imprisonment but may not impose the death penalty.
Harmon said Erdemovic, 24, had been the first Bosnian Serb Army insider to provide evidence in public about the killings in Srebrenica, a U.N. protected "safe area" in eastern Bosnia.
"His testimony exposed the lies of Bosnian Serb political and military leaders that the killings of civilians from Srebrenica was nothing but Moslem propaganda," he said.

Harmon was speaking at the end of a two-day pre-sentencing hearing in the case of Erdemovic who pleaded guilty in May to taking part in the slaughter of hundreds of unarmed Moslem men after Srebrenica fell to the Bosnian Serbs.
Erdemovic, who is expected to be sentenced within the next few weeks, told the tribunal he would have been killed himself if he had defied orders to shoot the Moslem prisoners.
U.N. war crimes prosecutors allege that Bosnian Serb forces summarily executed thousands of Moslem men after seizing Srebrenica.
Erdemovic said his unit of the Bosnian Serb Army had shot dead some 1,200 men who were taken in buses to a farm at Pilica near the town of Zvornik.
The tribunal has charged deposed Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic with genocide over the Srebrenica massacre.
But both men remain at large in common with the majority of the 75 suspects indicted by the tribunal.
